title: Teaching
text:
Course Websites
Two of my courses have their own websites with all the material in one place, from the slides to the experiments and practice questions:

LiFi Project for Digitization and Programming, in which first-semester students build a device that sends files with light and learn along the way how computers represent, store, transfer and process information.
Artificial Intelligence for Problem Solving with Artificial Intelligence and Applications of Artificial Intelligence, which explains how an AI agent works, from the language model inside it down to the idea of learning from data, with an experiment in every session.

title: Research
text:
Started in October 2026. FLEX3 develops a mobile, easy-to-use solution to stream lectures live, translate them into other languages with AI, and record them automatically. The transcripts then serve to generate summaries – including in plain language –, quizzes, and task lists. FLEX3 is one of three pilot projects selected from 17 proposals in the university’s Flexcellence program; I am its spokesperson.

Project Website




Within this project, my team and I explore how an AI-based virtual shopping assistant can help in the context of contactless smart stores.

section: A Teaser for the LiFi Project
text:
A Teaser for the LiFi Project
In our first-semester module Digitization and Programming, students build a small device that sends a file from one laptop to another with nothing but light. This short teaser introduces the project, and it is my first attempt at a video that is entirely computer-animated: Claude Opus 5.5 wrote the code that draws every frame, while the voice, the music and the parrot artwork were generated with other AI tools.


  


Everything about the project is on the course website.

title: Prof. Dr. Nicolas Meseth
text:
Latest Project: FLEX3
I am curious about how AI can help make teaching more accessible and inclusive. In October 2026, I started exploring this topic in the project FLEX3, funded by the Flexcellence program of the University of Applied Sciences Osnabrück. Learn more on the official project page.
The project video introduces the idea in about seven minutes. It is in German with subtitles, and its opening also plays in English, Arabic and Ukrainian, dubbed with AI in my own voice.

AI in the video: dubbing of the opening and the voice of the animation with ElevenLabs, background image and music AI-generated.
One goal of this project is to create different AI-dubbed versions of the same lecture recording. The two videos below show an example from a Science Slam I held in 2025. The version on the left is the original German version, while the version on the right is an English dub created with ElevenLabs.io. The videos are available on YouTube.

title: Software
text: These are tools I built because I needed them in my own teaching and research. All of them are public on GitHub, and most are released under the MIT licence, so you are welcome to use and adapt them.

title: Software
text:
stagekit
Slide decks as HTML: one file per deck, drawings as SVG, live demonstrators embedded right on the slide, and the whole design taken from a single theme file. Decks build up step by step instead of animating, open speaker notes in a second window, offer a laser pointer, and export to PDF.
stagekit started in the LiFi Project and now carries my lectures and talks. It comes with a skill that lets an AI agent build new decks following its rules, so the design stays consistent from one deck to the next. You can see it at work on the course websites of the LiFi Project and Artificial Intelligence.
stagekit on GitHub · MIT licence

title: Software
text:
LabelBench
LabelBench evaluates classifiers against a gold standard and shows every result in a self-contained HTML report that domain experts can browse row by row. Because the classifier is interchangeable, a hand-written rule set and a large language model are run, evaluated and compared in exactly the same way, which shows within minutes whether a change helped and on which items it did not.
LabelBench on GitHub · MIT licence · version 0.3

title: Software
text:
Lecture Recorder
A small Windows app that records lectures locally with OBS Studio, built as a replacement for recording through Microsoft Teams. It captures screen, webcam and microphone in one go and afterwards files two synchronized videos, screen and camera, into a folder per term and module.






The setup window: module, screen, camera and microphone with a live level meter




While recording, the window shrinks to a slim bar and is never captured itself. The taskbar stays out of the picture, a hotkey pauses and resumes, and stopping first asks whether to keep the recording, so an accidental click costs nothing.




Lecture Recorder on GitHub · MIT licence

title: Software
text:
Markwise






In development.



A desktop app for paper exams: it keeps a bank of multiple-choice and free-text questions, builds exams from it, reads the scanned answer sheets and turns them into grades. Free-text answers are marked by hand on paper, with the points ticked in a box strip that the scan reads as well. Markwise runs natively on Windows, needs neither Linux nor LaTeX, and is meant for examiners without any technical background.
Markwise on GitHub
